29.summary: This rule explains what happens after a legal case is accepted by the tribunal. The accepted case is given a number and written down in a special book called a register. This helps keep track of the documents properly.
points: Appeals, petitions, caveats, and applications are registered after they are admitted.
Each accepted matter is given a specific number.
The number is entered into the correct official register.
29.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an application with the tribunal. Once the tribunal checked and accepted the application, it did not just leave the papers on a desk. Instead, the staff gave the application a unique number. They then wrote this number down in the official register book meant for such cases. This step ensured that Meera Textiles Private Limited's matter was officially recorded and easy to find later.

terms.meaning: when the tribunal accepts a case or document for hearing
an official book or record used to keep track of details

29.watch: Do not confuse this with filing a case, because registration happens only after the case is officially admitted.

30.summary: This rule explains that after an appeal, petition, or application is admitted, the Registrar can ask for the case records from a lower authority if the Tribunal tells them to do so. Once the records are used, the Registrar sends them back. The provided text is very brief, so this is all the information available.
points: The rule applies after an appeal, petition, or application is admitted.
The Registrar must be directed by the Tribunal to act.
The Registrar calls for records from any adjudicating authority.
The Registrar retransmits the records after use.
30.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an appeal with the Tribunal. The Tribunal wanted to check the history of the case from the lower adjudicating authority. Therefore, the Tribunal directed the Registrar to call for the records. The Registrar requested the files from the lower authority, and after the Tribunal finished reviewing them, the Registrar retransmitted the records back as per the rule.

terms.meaning: An official responsible for keeping records and managing administrative tasks for the Tribunal.
A lower body or authority that previously judged or handled the case.
To send something back to where it came from.

30.watch: A common confusion is thinking the Registrar can call for records on their own, but the rule requires a direct order from the Tribunal first.

31.summary: When an association files a legal case like an appeal or petition, the person signing it must show proof that they were chosen to do so. They must attach a copy of the association's resolution and a list of members who will benefit from the case. The Registrar can also ask for more proof of authorization at any time.
points: A true copy of the association resolution must be produced along with the filing for verification.
The filing must include a list of members for whose benefit the proceedings are instituted.
The Registrar may ask for further materials at any time to be satisfied about due authorization.
31.example: An association named Apex Welfare Association wants to file a petition before the Tribunal. Mr. Sharma signs the petition on behalf of the association. Along with the petition, Mr. Sharma must submit a true copy of the association's resolution empowering him to sign, and a list of all the members who will benefit from this legal proceeding. Later, the Registrar asks Mr. Sharma to provide more materials to double-check that he is truly authorized to act for the association.

terms.meaning: A formal decision passed by the members of an association.
The office that handles court or tribunal filings and records.
Official permission given to someone to do something.

31.watch: Do not forget to attach both the resolution copy and the member list when filing.

32.summary: This rule explains how to file a special request while a court case is already ongoing. You must use the right form, follow all required steps, and include an affidavit to support your request. These requests can be for things like a stay, a direction, or extra time.
points: Applies to pending matters before the tribunal.
Covers requests such as stay, direction, condonation of delay, exemption, or extension of time.
Must be made in a prescribed form.
Requires an affidavit to support the application.
32.example: Asha Pharma Private Limited is involved in a pending company case. The company needs more time to submit a document. To ask for this, Asha Pharma must file an Interlocutory Application using the official prescribed form. They must also follow all specific rules for this request and submit a supporting affidavit alongside the form.

terms.meaning: A request made to the court or tribunal for an order during the course of an ongoing case.
A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation, used as evidence.
Official forgiveness or excuse of a delay in meeting a deadline.

32.watch: Do not forget that a supporting affidavit is mandatory for every such application.

33.summary: This rule explains what happens when a document submitted with a court paper is damaged or in poor condition. The person submitting it must note its bad condition in the index of the paper. Then, the official who receives the paper must check and sign next to that note.
points: Check if any document submitted with your pleading is defaced, torn, or damaged.
Mention the bad condition of the document in the index of your pleading.
The authorized receiving officer will verify and sign your note about the document.
33.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited submitted a legal pleading along with several documents to the Tribunal. One of the attached contracts was partially torn. Following the rules, Meera Textiles noted the torn condition of the contract in the index of their pleading. When the receiving officer accepted the paperwork, the officer inspected the torn contract and placed their initials next to the note in the index to confirm they saw it.

terms.meaning: a formal legal document filed in a case that states a party's claims or defenses
a list at the beginning of a document that shows what papers are included
signed with just one's initials rather than the full name

33.watch: Do not forget to write the note in the index yourself before submitting the damaged document.

34.summary: This rule explains the basic steps and forms you must use when bringing a matter before the Tribunal. If a specific situation is not covered by the rules, the Tribunal will decide the procedure fairly and write down its reasons. All papers must also follow the correct standard formats and be verified by an affidavit.
points: The Tribunal can decide its own fair procedure for any situation not covered by the existing rules, and it must record its reasons in writing.
All proceedings, advertisements, and notices must use the general heading in Form No. NCLT. 4.
Petitions, applications, and references must be filed in specific forms with required attachments.
Every petition, application, and interlocutory application must be verified by an affidavit in Form No. NCLT. 6.
34.example: Aarav wanted to file a case on behalf of Aero Motors Private Limited before the Tribunal. He made sure to check the required paperwork. He prepared his petition using Form No. NCLT. 1 and attached the necessary documents along with Form No. NCLT. 2. He also included a signed affidavit in Form No. NCLT. 6 to verify that his statements were true. Because the rules did not cover a specific unique issue that came up during the filing, the Tribunal wrote down its reasons and decided the procedure fairly according to natural justice.

terms.meaning: A special body or court set up to handle company law disputes.
A request made to the Tribunal during the middle of an ongoing case for a temporary order.
A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence.

34.watch: Do not confuse a regular petition or application with an interlocutory application, as they require different accompanying forms.

35.summary: This rule explains how a company must publish a public notice about a petition filed before the Tribunal. The notice must appear in local and English newspapers at least fourteen days before the hearing, unless the Tribunal says otherwise. It must also contain specific details like the hearing date and how affected persons can respond.
points: Advertisements must be published in Form NCLT-3A at least fourteen days before the hearing date.
Notices must appear in one local language newspaper and one English newspaper in the company's district.
An affidavit with proof of publication must be filed with the Tribunal at least three days before the hearing.
If rules are not followed, the Tribunal may dismiss the petition or give new directions.
35.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a petition with the Tribunal. To follow the rules, the company published an advertisement in Form NCLT-3A in a local vernacular newspaper and an English newspaper fourteen days before the hearing date. The advertisement listed the presentation date, the company's address, the petition details, the hearing date, and instructions for affected persons to send notice. Meera Textiles then filed an affidavit with proof of the advertisements to the Tribunal at least three days before the hearing.

terms.meaning: A specialized legal body set up to handle company disputes and cases.
A newspaper printed in the local language of a specific region.
A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence.

35.watch: People often confuse the fourteen-day deadline for publishing the advertisement with the three-day deadline for filing the proof affidavit.

36.summary: This rule explains how the Registry must record money received through postal orders, demand drafts, or cash. The Registration Clerk enters the payment in a Cash Register right away. Later, these payments are checked, signed for by the Cashier, and deposited into the bank account of the Tribunal.
points: The Registration Clerk must immediately enter any cash, postal order, or demand draft received by the Registry into the Cash Register.
On the next working day or the last working day of the week, the clerk hands over the postal orders and demand drafts to the Cashier.
The Cashier checks the money and signs to show receipt in the Cash Register.
The Cashier deposits all the collected cash, postal orders, and demand drafts into the bank account of the Tribunal.
36.example: Aarav visited the Registry of the Tribunal to make a payment and handed over a demand draft. The Registration Clerk immediately wrote down this transaction on the receipt side of the Cash Register. On the next working day, the clerk sent the demand draft to the official handling cashier work. After checking the details, the cashier signed the Cash Register to acknowledge the money and then safely deposited the demand draft into the official bank account of the Tribunal.

terms.meaning: The office where documents and payments are received and filed for the Tribunal.
A specialized official body set up to handle legal cases and disputes.
A prepaid negotiable instrument issued by a bank to guarantee payment.

36.watch: Do not confuse the Registration Clerk, who makes the first entry, with the Cashier, who verifies and deposits the money into the bank.

37.summary: When someone files a petition at the Tribunal, the Tribunal sends a notice to the respondent to show cause. If the respondent does not show up after getting a fair chance, the Tribunal will move ahead without them. If the respondent wants to fight the case, they must file a reply with documents before the hearing.
points: The Tribunal sends Form No. NCLT. 5 to the respondent with a copy of the application and supporting documents.
If the respondent is absent on the hearing date and has had a fair chance, the Tribunal handles the case ex-parte.
A contesting respondent can file a reply with an affidavit and documents in person or through an authorised representative.
The reply must be given to the Registry and the petitioner in advance before the hearing date.
37.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a petition against Alpha Industries Limited at the Tribunal. The Tribunal issued a notice in Form No. NCLT. 5 with the petition copy to Alpha Industries Limited for a specific hearing date. Alpha Industries Limited decided to contest the case. Their authorised representative prepared a reply with an affidavit and supporting documents, sent an advance copy to Meera Textiles Private Limited, and filed it with the Registry before the hearing date.

terms.meaning: The judicial body or authority handling the case.
Proceeding with the case without the other party present.
A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence.

37.watch: People often confuse missing a hearing with being excused, but the Tribunal will proceed without the respondent if they simply fail to appear after a fair chance.

38.summary: This rule explains how the Tribunal sends notices and processes to parties involved in a case. It allows service through post, courier, email, hand delivery, or directly by the party. The Tribunal can also direct alternative methods of service if needed.
points: Notices may be sent by post, courier, or email address given in the petition or reply.
Physical service can be done by hand delivery, registered post, speed post, courier, or by the party themselves.
When a party serves the notice themselves, they must file proof of delivery and an affidavit of service with the Registrar.
The Tribunal can direct alternative or substituted service if regular service is not possible.
Service can also be properly made on an authorised representative of a party.
38.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a petition before the Tribunal against another company. The Tribunal directed Meera Textiles to serve the notice by hand delivery through its authorised representative. After delivering the documents, Meera Textiles obtained the acknowledgment and filed it along with an affidavit of service with the Registrar of the Tribunal, fulfilling the legal requirement.

terms.meaning: A specialized legal body set up to handle specific disputes under the law.
A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence.
A person or agency which delivers the document and provides proof of its delivery.

38.watch: People often confuse personal service by a party with lack of proper proof, but the law strictly requires filing an affidavit and proof of delivery.

38A.summary: This rule explains how a legal request, called a petition, must be set up under the law. It states that each petition can only deal with one main reason for bringing the case. However, it allows you to ask for multiple forms of help, as long as those forms of help naturally follow from the main reason.
points: A petition must focus on only one cause of action.
You can ask for more than one relief in that same petition.
Any extra reliefs you ask for must be consequential to one another.
38A.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a legal request with the tribunal because a rival company illegally copied their unique clothing design. In their single petition, Meera Textiles asked the tribunal to officially stop the rival company from selling the copied design. They also asked the tribunal to order the rival company to hand over all profits made from selling those copied clothes, as this second request directly followed the first one.

terms.meaning: The main reason or set of facts that gives you the right to go to court or tribunal.
The different types of help or remedies that you ask the tribunal to give you.
Resulting directly from another event or action.

38A.watch: A common confusion is thinking you can mix completely unrelated complaints into one petition, but the rules require the reliefs to be consequential.

39.summary: The National Company Law Tribunal can ask parties to present their evidence using a written and sworn statement called an affidavit. If needed for fairness, the Tribunal may also order the person who wrote the statement to be questioned by the other side. Every affidavit must be filed using a specific official form.
points: The Tribunal may direct parties to provide evidence by affidavit.
The Tribunal can order cross-examination of the person giving the affidavit if it is necessary for fairness.
Cross-examination can happen through video conferencing or other methods decided by the Tribunal upon request.
Every affidavit filed before the Tribunal must use Form No. NCLT. 7.
39.example: A dispute arose at Aarav Industries Private Limited regarding a contract. The Tribunal asked both sides to give their evidence by affidavit using Form No. NCLT. 7. Later, one party felt that a statement in the affidavit was unclear and unfair. They applied to the Tribunal for a chance to question the person who wrote the statement. The Tribunal agreed and ordered a cross-examination through video conferencing to ensure fairness.

terms.meaning: A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation, used as evidence in court.
A person who makes an affidavit.
The questioning of a witness called by the other party.

39.watch: People often confuse regular written letters with official affidavits, but affidavits must strictly follow the required form.

40.summary: Generally, parties cannot bring new evidence before the Bench if they already had it during a government investigation into the company but did not show it then. However, the Bench can allow new evidence, witnesses, or documents if it needs them to pass an order, if there is a strong reason, or if the investigator did not give the party enough chance to present their case. The opposing side must also get a chance to see and challenge this new evidence.
points: Parties cannot normally submit new evidence to the Bench that they kept back during the government investigation.
The Bench can permit new evidence, witnesses, or documents if it needs them to pass orders or for a substantial cause.
The Bench can also allow new evidence if the investigator did not give the party a fair chance to present it.
The other parties involved must be given an opportunity to see and counter the new evidence.
40.example: During an investigation of Alpha Electronics Private Limited, Raj held back a key document. Later, before the Bench, Raj tries to submit it. Normally, he cannot do this because he had it during the investigation. However, if the Bench decides it needs this document to make a proper decision, or if Raj proves the investigator never gave him a fair chance to show it earlier, the Bench may allow him to submit it. If allowed, the opposing party will get a copy to review and challenge.

terms.meaning: A panel of judges or tribunal members hearing the case.
To produce or present evidence.
To argue against, disprove, or challenge something.

40.watch: Do not assume parties are always banned from bringing new evidence; exceptions exist if the Bench orders it or if the prior investigator was unfair.

41.summary: Rule 41 explains how a respondent must respond to a petition or application in the Tribunal. The respondent needs to file a reply, along with relevant documents, at the registry and also share copies with the applicant immediately. In this reply, the respondent must clearly address the facts presented by the applicant.
points: The respondent can file their reply and documents in person or through an authorised person at the Tribunal registry.
A copy of the reply and documents must be sent to the applicant right away.
The reply must specifically admit, deny, or contest the facts stated by the applicant and can include any necessary additional facts.
41.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an application against Rohan Sharma at the Tribunal. According to the rules, Rohan must now file his reply and supporting documents at the Tribunal registry. At the same time, Rohan must immediately send a copy of his reply and documents directly to Meera Textiles Private Limited. In his written reply, Rohan needs to clearly state which of their claims he accepts or denies, and he can also add any extra facts that are important for his case.

terms.meaning: The person or company against whom a legal petition or application has been filed.
The person or company that has filed the petition or application.
The official administrative office of the Tribunal where documents are filed.

41.watch: Do not forget that you must share your reply with the applicant immediately, not just file it with the Tribunal.

42.summary: This rule explains when a petitioner can file a rejoinder. If the respondent brings up new facts needed for a fair decision, the Bench can allow the petitioner to reply. The petitioner must also send an advance copy of this reply to the respondent.
points: The respondent may state additional facts for a just decision.
The Bench may allow the petitioner to file a rejoinder to the reply.
An advance copy of the rejoinder must be served on the respondent.
42.example: In a dispute before the National Company Law Tribunal involving Meera Textiles Private Limited, the respondent brought up new facts in their reply. Because these facts were important for a just decision, the Bench allowed the petitioner to file a rejoinder. Before submitting it to the Bench, the petitioner made sure to send an advance copy of the rejoinder directly to the respondent.

terms.meaning: a written reply given by the petitioner to the answer provided by the respondent
a panel of judges or tribunal members hearing the case

42.watch: A rejoinder is only for addressing new facts brought up by the respondent, not for repeating the original petition.

43.summary: The National Company Law Tribunal bench has the power to ask for more documents and evidence before it makes a final decision on a case. It can also accept electronic records like emails and digital files during an inquiry or investigation. If someone claims records are fake in an oppression and mismanagement case, they can ask for a forensic test.
points: The Bench can demand extra documents or evidence from any party before making an order.
The Bench can accept electronic evidence like emails, accounts, and contracts.
Parties can ask for a forensic examination from the Central Forensic Science Laboratory if they claim records are forged.
43.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited was involved in a company dispute. During the court hearing, the judges felt they needed more details to understand the truth of the claims. The Bench used its power to ask both parties to submit extra documents. Later, a shareholder claimed that certain account books were fake. That shareholder applied for a forensic test, and the Bench decided to send the disputed records to the Central Forensic Science Laboratory for an expert opinion at the shareholder's expense.

terms.meaning: A panel of judges or tribunal members hearing a case.
Scientific tests done on items like documents to check if they are fake.

43.watch: People often think forensic tests are free, but the party claiming forgery must pay for the Central Forensic Science Laboratory opinion.

44.summary: This rule explains how hearing dates are given and how a case can be withdrawn. The Tribunal will tell the parties when and where their hearing will happen. If an applicant wants to cancel their request before the hearing, they must ask the Tribunal and may have to pay costs.
points: The Tribunal notifies parties about the hearing date and place.
An applicant can ask to withdraw their petition or application before the hearing.
The Tribunal may allow the withdrawal and order costs for fairness.
44.example: Aarav filed a petition at the National Company Law Tribunal on behalf of Zenith Solutions Private Limited. Later, Aarav decided to stop the case before the hearing started. He submitted an official request to the Tribunal to withdraw the petition. The Tribunal reviewed his request, heard his arguments, and permitted the withdrawal while ordering him to pay certain costs in the interest of justice.

terms.meaning: The judicial body that handles company law cases.
The person or company that files a request or petition.
Money ordered to be paid by a party, often for expenses related to the case.

44.watch: Do not assume there is a specific deadline or amount for costs, as the text does not state any.

45.summary: This rule explains how parties can appear and be represented before the Tribunal under the Companies Act, 2013. It outlines who can represent different parties, how that representative must formally enter an appearance, and the Tribunal's power to request company information. Additionally, it bans audio and video recording of the proceedings.
points: A party can appear in person or through an authorised representative with written permission.
Representatives must file a specific form or Vakalatnama to make their appearance.
Government authorities can send certain officers or advocates to represent them.
The Tribunal can ask the Registrar of Companies for information based on the MCA21 portal, with written reasons.
Audio and video recording of the bench proceedings by parties or representatives is strictly prohibited.
45.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited is involved in a case before the Tribunal. Instead of attending personally, the company gives written authority to an authorised representative. To officially represent them in the proceedings, this representative files a Memorandum of Appearance in Form No. NCLT. 12. During the hearing, neither Meera Textiles nor their representative is allowed to make any audio or video recording of the bench proceedings. Meanwhile, the Tribunal requests the Registrar of Companies to submit information on the company using the MCA21 portal, after recording its reasons in writing.

terms.meaning: A written document by which a client gives a lawyer or representative the authority to act on their behalf.
A special official body set up to deal with specific legal disputes and cases.
An officer appointed to handle the winding up or closing down of a company.

45.watch: People often assume they can record the Tribunal hearings on their phones, but the rule completely bans any audio or video recording by parties.

46.summary: An intern working for an authorised representative cannot appear before the Tribunal or access its records unless their name is registered. The authorised representative must apply to the Registrar using Form NCLT 10 to get the intern's name added to the official register. This ensures only registered interns are permitted to work with the Tribunal files and representatives.
points: Interns must be listed in the Tribunal's register of interns before they can act or access records.
The authorised representative must file an application to the Registrar using Form NCLT 10.
The Registrar must allow the application before the intern's name is added to the register.
46.example: Mr. Sharma is an authorised representative for Meera Textiles Private Limited at the Tribunal. He wants his intern, Rohan, to help him by getting copies of Tribunal orders. Before Rohan can do this, Mr. Sharma must apply to the Registrar using Form NCLT 10. Once the Registrar allows this application, Rohan's name will be entered in the register of interns. After this process, Rohan is officially permitted to access the records of the Tribunal bench where Mr. Sharma ordinarily appears.

terms.meaning: A specialized legal body established to handle company law disputes.
A person permitted to present a case or act on behalf of someone else before the Tribunal.
An official officer responsible for maintaining the records and administrative work of the Tribunal.

46.watch: Remember that an intern cannot simply start working at the Tribunal without their name first being entered into the register through the proper application.

47.summary: This rule explains how a witness must promise to tell the truth before speaking in front of the Tribunal. A special officer will make the witness swear in the name of God or solemnly affirm. The witness must promise that their statements will be the absolute truth.
points: A Bench Officer or Court Officer administers the oath.
The witness can swear in the name of God or solemnly affirm.
The witness must promise to tell the truth and nothing but the truth.
47.example: At the National Company Law Tribunal, a dispute arose involving Zenith Foods Private Limited. Mr. Rao was called to speak about the company affairs. Before he began his statement, the Court Officer stepped forward. The officer asked Mr. Rao to take the required oath. Mr. Rao chose to solemnly affirm. He stated that what he would say shall be the truth and nothing but the truth.

terms.meaning: A solemn promise to tell the truth.
A person who gives statements or evidence.
To make a formal and serious declaration without swearing on God.

47.watch: People often confuse whether an oath must be religious, but the rule allows for a solemn affirmation instead.

48.summary: This rule explains what happens when a person who filed a request at the Tribunal does not show up for the hearing. The Tribunal can either dismiss the request or decide the case anyway. If the request is dismissed, the applicant can ask to restore it within thirty days by showing a good reason for missing the hearing.
points: If the applicant is absent on the hearing date, the Tribunal may dismiss the case or decide it on its merits.
The applicant can file a request within thirty days to restore a dismissed case.
The applicant must prove there was a good reason for not being present.
If the Tribunal already decided the case on its merits, it cannot be reopened.
48.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an application with the Tribunal. On the day of the hearing, the director of Meera Textiles Private Limited missed the appearance due to a sudden medical emergency. Because of this absence, the Tribunal dismissed the application for default. Within thirty days, Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a new application explaining the medical emergency and satisfied the Tribunal. The Tribunal then made an order restoring the case.

terms.meaning: A specialized official body set up to handle legal disputes and applications under the law.
Postponed to another date.
Failure to appear or act as required.

48.watch: A case dismissed for default can be restored within thirty days, but a case decided on its merits can never be reopened.

49.summary: This rule explains what happens if only one party shows up for a legal hearing at the Tribunal. If the applicant comes but the respondent does not, the Tribunal can either postpone the case or decide it without the respondent. The absent respondent can later ask to cancel this decision if they prove they did not get proper notice or had a valid reason for missing it.
points: If the applicant appears and the respondent does not on the hearing date, the Tribunal may postpone the hearing or decide the case ex-parte.
An absent respondent can apply to the Tribunal to set aside the ex-parte decision.
The respondent must satisfy the Tribunal that they were not duly served notice or were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing.
If the decision cannot be set aside for just one respondent, the Tribunal may set it aside for all or any of the other respondents.
49.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an application against Alpha Industries Private Limited at the Tribunal. On the hearing day, the representative of Meera Textiles Private Limited was present, but no one appeared for Alpha Industries Private Limited when the case was called. The Tribunal chose to hear and decide the matter ex-parte. Later, Alpha Industries Private Limited applied to the Tribunal, proving they never received the notice for the hearing. The Tribunal accepted their reason and made an order setting aside the ex-parte decision against them.

terms.meaning: Done with only one side present and participating, without the other side.
Postponed or delayed to another date.
The party against whom a petition or application is filed.

49.watch: Do not assume a missed hearing is always decided immediately, as the Tribunal has the option to simply postpone the case instead.

50.summary: The Registry must give a free certified copy of the final order to the people involved in the case. If anyone needs certified copies in other cases, they have to pay a fee based on the official fee schedule. This rule ensures parties receive their final orders properly.
points: The Registry sends a certified copy of the final order to the concerned parties for free.
Certified copies for all other cases are provided with a cost according to the Schedule of fees.
50.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited was involved in a legal dispute at the Tribunal. After the final order was passed, the Registry prepared a certified copy. Because this was the final order, the Registry sent it to Meera Textiles Private Limited free of cost. Later, the company needed an extra copy of a different document related to the case. For this other document, the Registry charged them a cost as per the Schedule of fees.

terms.meaning: The office responsible for keeping records and handling administrative work for the Tribunal.
An official copy of a document that is stamped and signed as a true copy of the original.

50.watch: Do not assume that all copies are free, because only the final order given to the concerned parties is free of cost.

51.summary: This rule gives the Tribunal the power to decide its own procedures. It must follow basic fairness and justice while doing its work. This helps the Tribunal handle its duties properly.
points: The Tribunal can set its own way of working.
It must follow the rules of natural justice and equity.
This power is used to discharge functions under the Act.
51.example: A dispute arose at Ananya Enterprises Private Limited, and the case went to the Tribunal. The Tribunal needed to decide how to schedule the hearings and review documents. Based on the rules, the Tribunal set its own step-by-step procedure to hear both sides fairly, ensuring that natural justice was maintained while it carried out its official functions.

terms.meaning: A special body set up to solve legal disputes.
Basic rules of fairness that everyone must follow.
Fairness and impartiality in treatment.

51.watch: Do not assume the Tribunal can ignore basic fairness just because it sets its own procedure.

52.summary: Under this rule, parties involved in a case before the Tribunal can ask for witnesses to be called. The Tribunal will issue the summons unless it believes the witness is not needed for a fair decision. The person asked to appear is entitled to travel and daily allowances determined and deposited by the party.
points: A party to a proceeding can apply to summon witnesses.
The Tribunal issues the summons unless it decides the witness is unnecessary.
Summoned witnesses get travel and daily allowances for their expenses.
The Registrar decides the allowance amount and who deposits it.
52.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited is involved in a case before the Tribunal. They want a former manager to testify and present records. Meera Textiles applies for a witness summons. The Tribunal agrees the witness is necessary and issues the summons. Following the rules, the Registrar decides the travel expenses for the witness. Meera Textiles then deposits this amount so the witness can attend without personal financial loss.

terms.meaning: The judicial body or authority handling the legal case.
An official order telling someone to appear in court or produce documents.
An administrative officer of the Tribunal.

52.watch: People often confuse who pays the witness expenses, but the party asking for the witness must deposit the amount decided by the Registrar.

53.summary: This rule explains what happens to a legal case at the Tribunal if a party dies, becomes bankrupt, or a company goes through winding up. The case does not end automatically, but can continue with the proper representatives. However, if a party dies, their legal representative must ask to join the case within ninety days.
points: A legal case does not stop if a party dies, becomes insolvent, or a company is wound up.
The executor, administrator, receiver, or liquidator can continue the case.
A dead party's legal representative must apply to join the record within ninety days of the death.
The case will end if no one applies within ninety days, unless the Tribunal allows it for good reasons.
53.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited was involved in a legal case before the Tribunal. During the proceedings, the sole owner of Meera Textiles Private Limited sadly passed away. According to the rules, the case did not automatically abate. Within ninety days, the appointed executor of the owner applied to the Tribunal to be brought on record as the legal representative. The Tribunal accepted the application, and the legal proceedings were allowed to continue smoothly with the executor representing the company's interests.

terms.meaning: To stop or end completely.
Unable to pay debts.
The official body handling these legal proceedings.

53.watch: People often confuse the automatic ending of a case after ninety days with a final permanent closure, but the Tribunal can still allow substitution later for good reasons.

54.summary: This rule allows the Tribunal to get help from experts during an enquiry into a claim. The Tribunal can bring in up to two assessors or valuers who have special technical knowledge. The Tribunal also decides what work these experts will do and how much they will be paid.
points: The Tribunal can call up to two assessors or valuers for help in an enquiry.
These experts must have special or technical knowledge about the matter.
The Tribunal tells the assessors or valuers what functions to perform.
The Tribunal fixes and pays the remuneration for the assessors or valuers.
54.example: During an enquiry into a claim involving Meera Textiles Private Limited, the Tribunal needed help understanding complex factory machinery. To do this, the Tribunal called in two technical experts as assessors. The Tribunal told them to inspect the factory and explain how the machinery worked. Finally, the Tribunal decided what payment these two experts would receive and how it would be paid to them.

terms.meaning: A legal body established to handle and decide cases.
An expert with special or technical knowledge who helps the Tribunal.
Payment or money given for work or services done.

54.watch: People often confuse the Tribunal with a regular court, but this rule specifically applies to the National Company Law Tribunal.

55.summary: This rule explains that you cannot submit extra written arguments after the initial reply unless the Tribunal permits it. The Tribunal can set its own conditions if it decides to allow these extra papers. Without this special permission, no further documents are allowed.
points: No further pleadings are allowed after the reply.
You can only submit them if the Tribunal gives you leave.
The Tribunal may set specific terms when granting permission.
55.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a case at the Tribunal. After the opposing party submitted their reply, Meera Textiles wanted to present an additional written document. Because of the rules, they could not just file it. They had to ask the Tribunal for permission first. The Tribunal reviewed the request and granted leave on specific terms, allowing Meera Textiles Private Limited to finally present their subsequent pleading.

terms.meaning: Written statements or documents filed by parties in a legal case.
Official permission to do something.

55.watch: People often think they can submit as many written replies as they want, but you always need the Tribunal's permission for anything after the first reply.

56.summary: This rule explains how to carry out an order given by the Tribunal. If you hold an order, you must apply to the Tribunal using a specific form. The text is very short, so it only tells you the required form name without extra details.
points: You must apply to the Tribunal to execute an order.
The application must be made using Form NCLT.8.
56.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited received a favorable order from the Tribunal against a vendor. To make sure the vendor actually follows the order, Meera Textiles Private Limited needs to start the enforcement process. According to the rules, the company must fill out Form NCLT.8 and submit this application directly to the Tribunal to carry out the order.

terms.meaning: A specialized legal body set up to handle specific types of cases.
The process of carrying out or enforcing an official order.
The specific official document required to request the execution of an order.

56.watch: Do not assume there are extra steps or deadlines since the text does not mention any.

57.summary: When the Tribunal gets an application to enforce an order, it uses a specific legal form to start the process. The Tribunal will also look at any objections from the other side before deciding what to do next. Finally, it may issue a warrant to attach property or recover money using the proper forms.
points: The Tribunal starts the execution process after receiving an application.
The Tribunal considers any objections raised by the respondent.
The Tribunal can issue an attachment or recovery warrant.
57.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an application with the Tribunal to enforce an official order against a debtor. The debtor raised an objection against this action. The Tribunal carefully considered the debtor's objection and decided to move forward. Afterward, the Tribunal issued a recovery warrant using the correct legal form to collect the dues.

terms.meaning: The person or company that answers to the application or complaint.
A legal process to seize property.

57.watch: Do not assume there is a fixed time period to raise objections, as the text does not mention one.

58.summary: Making a mistake or failing to follow a rule in these guidelines does not automatically cancel a legal proceeding. The proceeding stays valid unless the Tribunal decides that the mistake caused a miscarriage of justice. This protects cases from being thrown out over minor errors.
points: Failing to follow a rule does not automatically cancel a proceeding.
The proceeding remains valid despite the mistake.
The Tribunal can intervene only if the failure leads to a miscarriage of justice.
58.example: Asha Pharma Private Limited filed a petition with the Tribunal but forgot to format a document exactly as the rules described. The opposing party asked the Tribunal to throw out the entire case because of this mistake. The Tribunal checked the error and decided it did not cause any unfairness or miscarriage of justice. Therefore, the Tribunal allowed the proceeding to continue without canceling it.

terms.meaning: A specialized legal body set up to handle specific types of disputes.
A serious failure that leads to an unfair legal outcome.

58.watch: People often think any small procedural mistake will automatically cancel a legal case, but it only matters if it causes an unfair outcome.

59.summary: Under this rule, a penalty under the Companies Act cannot be decided against anyone without a proper notice and a chance to speak. The Registrar will send a notice giving at least fifteen days to reply in writing. Afterward, the Bench will decide the penalty based on the facts after looking at the reply and any oral hearing.
points: No penalty order can be made without giving a show cause notice and a fair chance to present the case.
The Registrar sends the show cause notice giving at least fifteen days to reply in writing.
The Bench makes the final decision on the penalty after receiving the written explanation and any oral hearing.
59.example: The National Company Law Tribunal wanted to impose a penalty on Meera Textiles Private Limited for a procedural fault. Instead of acting immediately, the Registrar issued a show cause notice to the company, giving them sixteen days to submit their written explanation. Meera Textiles submitted their reply on time. The Bench reviewed their written explanation, considered the facts of the case, and then decided the matter without bypassing their right to be heard.

terms.meaning: A formal notice asking a person or company to explain why an action should not be taken against them.
A panel of judges or tribunal members hearing a case.
An official responsible for keeping records and issuing official notices.

59.watch: A common confusion is thinking a penalty can be given without a written reply or hearing, but the rule requires giving at least fifteen days to submit an explanation.

61.summary: This rule allows the Tribunal to let outside experts or bodies share their views on legal issues as a friend of the court. These helpers can look at case documents, and the Tribunal can ask the parties in the case to pay their fees and expenses. Finally, the final judgment and any opinions are sent to both the parties and the helper.
points: The Tribunal can allow any person or professional body to act as an amicus curiae to give views on legal issues.
The amicus curiae is allowed to see the case pleadings submitted by the parties.
The Tribunal can order one or both parties to pay the fees and expenses of the amicus curiae.
The final judgment and opinions are sent to the parties and the amicus curiae.
61.example: A complex legal dispute arises at Meera Textiles Private Limited before the Tribunal. To help understand a tricky legal point, the Tribunal appoints an outside legal expert as an amicus curiae. The expert gets access to the case documents and submits a brief of their views. The Tribunal gives the parties time to reply to this brief. Afterward, the Tribunal orders Meera Textiles Private Limited to pay the expert's expenses and eventually sends the final judgment to both the company and the expert.

terms.meaning: A person or body permitted by the Tribunal to give views or opinions on legal issues.
The written documents and statements submitted by the parties involved in a case.

61.watch: People often confuse an amicus curiae with a lawyer hired by one of the parties, but they are actually an independent helper appointed by the Tribunal.

62.summary: This rule explains when a judge or leader of the Tribunal must step away from a case to keep fairness high. They must step aside if they have a personal or past professional connection to the people involved, if they worked on the same case before, or if joining in would seem wrong. They can write down why they stepped away, but no one involved in the case has a right to know those reasons.
points: The President or a Member of the Tribunal must step away from cases involving people they know personally, familially, or professionally.
They must step away if they previously helped with the case as an advisor, expert, witness, or representative.
They must step away if any other situation makes their participation seem inappropriate.
They may write down the reasons for stepping away, but people involved in the case do not have the right to know these reasons.
62.example: Mr. Sharma is a Member of the Tribunal assigned to hear a dispute involving Meera Textiles Private Limited. He realizes that the director of Meera Textiles is his close personal friend. To maintain integrity, Mr. Sharma must recuse himself and step away from the case. He may choose to record his reasons for stepping away in a note. However, neither Meera Textiles nor the opposing party has the legal right to demand or know why Mr. Sharma decided to step down.

terms.meaning: To step down or withdraw from judging a case to ensure complete fairness.
An official body set up to deal with specific legal disputes.

62.watch: People often think they can demand to know why a judge stepped aside, but the rule clearly states that parties have no right to know the reasons.

63.summary: This rule explains what you can do if you are unhappy with a decision made by the Registrar during the checking of petitions or applications. You can file an appeal against their order within fifteen days. The appeal goes to the President of the Principal Bench or a designated Member, and their decision will be final.
points: Applies when someone is aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar during scrutiny.
An appeal must be made within fifteen days of the order.
The appeal is submitted to the President of the Principal Bench or a designated Member.
The decision made on the appeal is final.
63.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a petition with the tribunal. The Registrar reviewed the petition and made a decision that left the company feeling unsatisfied. Because Meera Textiles Private Limited disagreed with the Registrar's order, they decided to challenge it. They filed an appeal within fifteen days to the President of the Principal Bench, whose decision on the matter will be final.

terms.meaning: A careful and thorough examination or inspection.
Feeling resentful or unfairly treated because of an official decision.
An official responsible for keeping records and handling administrative duties.

63.watch: People often confuse the fifteen-day deadline for appealing to the President or designated Member with other deadlines not mentioned in this rule.

65.summary: This rule states that the standard rules of the National Company Law Tribunal apply in the same way to certain special petitions or applications. Specifically, this covers requests made under section 45QA(2) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, or similar parts of other laws. In short, the usual tribunal procedures must be followed for these specific cases.
points: The tribunal rules apply to applications made under section 45QA(2) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
These same rules also apply to similar provisions found in other Acts.
The application of these rules follows a special procedure outlined in Part VIII.
65.example: Asha Finance Private Limited decided to file a special petition under section 45QA(2) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The company director wondered which procedural guidelines to follow for the court filing. Based on the rule, Asha Finance Private Limited must use the standard National Company Law Tribunal rules, applying them in the same manner as intended for these specific types of petitions.

terms.meaning: With necessary changes having been made, meaning that the rules apply similarly while adjusting minor details to fit the new situation.
A formal written request made to an official body or court for a particular action.
Comparable or similar in certain respects.

65.watch: A common confusion is assuming these rules change the core laws, whereas they only dictate the procedure for handling the application.

76.summary: If a member asks a company to inspect the minute-book of a general meeting and pays the required fee, but the company refuses, the member can take action. They can apply to the Tribunal using a specific form to get a direction forcing the company to allow the inspection.
points: A member must first request the inspection of the minute-book of a general meeting.
The member must pay the required fee for this inspection.
If the company refuses the request, the member can apply to the Tribunal.
The application to the Tribunal is made using Form No NCLT-9 to ask for a direction for inspection.
76.example: At Alpha Ventures Private Limited, a shareholder named Rohan paid the required fee and asked to inspect the minute-book of a recent general meeting. The company refused to show him the book. Because of this refusal, Rohan applied to the Tribunal using Form No NCLT-9 to request an official direction ordering Alpha Ventures Private Limited to let him inspect the minute-book.

terms.meaning: A special legal body or court that handles company law disputes.
An official book where a company records the discussions and decisions made at its meetings.
A shareholder or person who belongs to the company.

76.watch: Do not assume you can go directly to the Tribunal without first asking the company and paying the fee.

89.summary: This rule explains how the Registry must prepare and publish the daily cause list for the National Company Law Tribunal. It sets a specific order of priority for listing cases and details what information must be included in the list. Everyone can check the notice board before the office closes to see the schedule for the next working day.
points: The Registry must prepare and publish the cause list on its notice board before closing on each working day for the next working day.
Cases are listed in a specific order of priority, starting with orders, then clarifications, admissions, directions, part-heard cases, and finally numerical order.
The cause list must show the case number, day, date, time, court hall, and the names of the members forming the Bench.
The list must include the names of lawyers and their represented parties, or the names of unrepresented parties.
89.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited has a pending petition at the tribunal. To find out when their case will be heard tomorrow, their representative visits the tribunal office before closing hours. They check the notice board and find the daily cause list. The document clearly displays the date, court hall number, the names of the judges, and the lawyers representing both sides. Because their matter is listed for admission, they can easily locate it under the correct priority order.

terms.meaning: The administrative office of the tribunal that handles paperwork and scheduling.
The specific judges or members sitting together to form a bench for a hearing.
Lawyers or advocates representing the parties in a case.

89.watch: People often confuse the order of priority, assuming cases are listed strictly on a first-come, first-served basis.

90.summary: This rule explains what happens to court cases when the National Company Law Tribunal bench cannot meet. If a holiday or surprise event stops the bench from working, the cases for that day automatically move to the next working day. If a bench member cannot make it, the Registrar will choose a new convenient date and post it on the notice board.
points: Cases scheduled for a day when the bench does not function move to the next working day.
This moved list is added to the cases already planned for that next working day.
If a specific bench member cannot attend, the Registrar reschedules the cases to a convenient date.
Rescheduling details and directions are displayed on the Registry notice board.
90.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited had a scheduled hearing at the Tribunal on a Tuesday. However, the bench could not function that day due to an unexpected holiday. According to the rules, the cause list for that Tuesday automatically became the cause list for the next working day, alongside the cases already planned for that day. Separately, when a bench member fell ill and could not attend another hearing, the Registrar adjourned that specific case to a new convenient date and posted the notice on the Registry notice board.

terms.meaning: A list of court cases scheduled to be heard on a specific day.
A panel of judges or tribunal members sitting together to hear cases.
An official responsible for keeping records and managing administrative tasks for the tribunal.

90.watch: Do not assume cases are automatically dismissed when a bench cancels; they are simply moved to a new date or the next working day.

91.summary: This rule explains how case diaries must be maintained in the Tribunal. A designated clerk must write these diaries clearly using a specific format for each case. These diaries track the history of the case, orders passed, and steps taken to carry out those orders.
points: The clerk-in-charge must keep diaries for appeals, petitions, or applications in a specified form.
Entries in the diaries must be written clearly and legibly.
The main file diary must record the case history and the substance of any orders made.
Execution proceedings need a complete record of all steps taken to enforce orders or rules.
The Deputy Registrar must check and initial the diary once every two weeks.
91.example: At Omkara Enterprises Private Limited, a clerk named Rahul is put in charge of maintaining case records for a pending petition. Rahul ensures he writes neatly in the diary, recording every important update, the history of the case, and the substance of the recent orders. Every two weeks, the Deputy Registrar reviews Rahul's diary and initials it to confirm it has been checked properly.

terms.meaning: Official written records tracking the day-to-day progress and history of a case.
Legal steps taken to make sure that a court or tribunal order is actually carried out.
An official in the Tribunal responsible for administrative and record-checking duties.

91.watch: Do not confuse the main file diary with ordinary personal notes, as it must strictly contain official case history and order summaries.

92.summary: This rule explains how an official record of all orders must be kept during any legal proceeding. The Court Master maintains this running sheet, which includes details like the case reference number and the date. All main orders must be in English and signed by the Tribunal Members, while simple routine orders can be signed by the Court Master.
points: The Court Master must maintain an order sheet for every proceeding to record all orders passed over time.
All orders must be written in English and signed by the Tribunal Members.
Routine orders, such as adjournments or calling for records, may be signed by the Court Master instead.
The order sheet must include the reference number, date, short cause title, and other details.
92.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an application before the Tribunal. The Court Master created an order sheet for the case, noting the reference number and date. When the Tribunal Members decided on a major hearing, they wrote the order in English and signed it. Later, when the case was simply postponed to another day, the Court Master signed that routine adjournment order directly on the sheet.

terms.meaning: An official officer who assists the Tribunal and helps manage court records and proceedings.
The official heading of a case that shows the names of the parties involved.
Temporarily delayed or postponed to a later date.

92.watch: People often confuse routine orders like adjournments, which the Court Master can sign, with main orders that must be signed by the Tribunal Members.

93.summary: This rule explains how the Court Master keeps an official record of daily court events called a court diary. They must write down what happens for every case listed for that day, including whether it is finished, postponed, or waiting for an order. This ensures there is a clear written history of every hearing.
points: The Court Master of the Bench must keep a readable court diary.
The diary records court proceedings for each daily sitting.
It covers all applications, petitions, and appeals listed for the day.
Entries must state if a case is adjourned, part-heard, disposed of, or has orders reserved.
93.example: At Zenith Enterprises Private Limited's hearing before the Tribunal, the Court Master opens the official court diary. Because the judges need more time to review the documents, the case is not finished today. The Court Master legibly writes down in the diary that the matter is adjourned, noting the specific date set for the next sitting, ensuring a complete and accurate record of today's proceedings.

terms.meaning: An official of the court responsible for managing courtroom proceedings and records.
Postponed to a later date.

93.watch: Do not confuse the daily cause list, which is the schedule of cases, with the court diary, which records what actually happened during those cases.

94.summary: This rule tells people involved in a legal case or their lawyers to give a special list before the daily court session starts. The list must show all law books, reports, laws, or photocopies they might need to use or look at during the hearing. They hand this list directly to the Court Master.
points: Applies to parties or their legal practitioners.
Must be done before the day's proceedings begin.
The list is given to the Court Master.
Includes law journals, reports, statutes, and citations or photocopies.
94.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited is involved in a case at the tribunal. Before the hearing starts for the day, their lawyer hands a list of law reports and statutes to the Court Master. This list shows the books and photocopies they plan to refer to during the arguments.

terms.meaning: Lawyers or advocates who represent people in court.
Written laws passed by a legislative body.
References to legal authorities or previously decided court cases.

94.watch: Do not forget that this list must be handed over before the proceedings start for the day.

95.summary: This rule explains the order in which court cases must be called during a hearing. Unless the Bench gives different instructions, the Court Master must call the cases in the exact order they appear on the cause list. This ensures an organized process for handling matters.
points: Cases are called by the Court Master.
The calling order follows the list serial numbers.
The Bench can change this order if needed.
95.example: At Sunrise Enterprises Private Limited, the directors are waiting for their company dispute to be heard. The Court Master follows the daily cause list and calls the cases one by one in their written serial order, unless the judges direct otherwise.

terms.meaning: An official list of cases scheduled to be heard by the court on a particular day.
An official who assists the judges and manages the daily court proceedings.

95.watch: Do not assume cases will always be called out of turn, as they normally follow the serial order.

96.summary: This rule explains how staff must keep the Tribunal running smoothly while it is in session. The Deputy Registrar and Court Master have specific duties to manage support staff, keep silence, and handle case records properly. It ensures that orders are quickly sent to the Registry and communicated to the right people.
points: The Deputy Registrar must make sure staff like stenographers and peons are ready so the Bench does not waste time.
The Court Master must keep complete silence and maintain the dignity of the court.
After an order is passed, the Court Master must send the case records to the Registry right away.
The Registry must check the records and quickly communicate the Tribunal's directions.
96.example: During a hearing at Meera Textiles Private Limited, the Court Master noticed whispering in the back of the room and immediately asked for quiet to keep the court's dignity. Once the Bench finished passing its order, the Court Master quickly sent the case file to the Registry. The Registry checked the file against the cause list and took steps to share the order right away.

terms.meaning: A specialized legal body set up to handle company disputes and cases.
An official staff member who helps manage the courtroom during a hearing.
The administrative office of the Tribunal where official case records are kept.

96.watch: Do not confuse the duties of the Deputy Registrar, who manages general staff availability, with the Court Master, who handles courtroom decorum and record handover.

97.summary: This rule explains that the Registry of the Tribunal must keep specific official registers. These registers need to be updated every single day. The Registrar decides which staff members will handle this duty, following any orders from the President.
points: The Registry of the Tribunal must maintain four specific registers.
Entries in these registers must be updated on a day-to-day basis.
The Registrar assigns staff members to maintain these registers based on orders from the President.
97.example: At Zenith Tribunal Private Limited Registry, officer Aarav was assigned by the Registrar, as per the President's orders, to update the office books. Every single day, Aarav carefully recorded all newly filed petitions, unnumbered appeals, lodged caveats, and interlocutory applications into their respective official registers without missing a single day.

terms.meaning: The administrative office of the Tribunal that handles paperwork and filings.
A formal notice given to a court or tribunal to prevent a certain step from being taken without previous notice.
A request made to the tribunal for an order during the course of legal proceedings.

97.watch: People often confuse the Registrar who manages the office staff with the President who gives overarching orders.

98.summary: This rule explains how records for pending matters in the National Company Law Tribunal must be organized. The case files are divided into four specific parts and kept in that order. This keeps all documents neat and easy to find.
points: Records must be divided into four parts.
The main file keeps the petition separately.
There is a miscellaneous application file.
There is a process file and an execution file.
98.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a petition in the tribunal. To follow the rules, the tribunal staff organized the paperwork carefully. They put the main petition in the main file and placed the other papers into the miscellaneous application file, the process file, and the execution file.

terms.meaning: collected and put in the correct order
a folder for papers related to carrying out the tribunal's orders

98.watch: Do not mix all the documents together, as they must be split into four distinct files.

99.summary: This rule explains how the main file of a case must be organized and kept safe. Every document must be placed in a specific order. It must be kept forever as a permanent record unless the rules say it can be destroyed.
points: The main file must follow a strict order of documents.
It starts with an index and order sheet, followed by the final judgment.
It includes the original petition, replies, all types of evidence, and written arguments.
The file must be kept as a permanent record until an order allows its destruction.
99.example: Asha Trading Private Limited filed a petition with the tribunal. When the case ended, the clerk had to organize the main case file properly. First came the index, then the order sheet, and the final judgment. Next were Asha Trading's petition, the reply from the other party, all the evidence, and the written arguments. The clerk stored this complete file safely as a permanent record, exactly as the rules require.

terms.meaning: The official written request or complaint that starts a case.
The written answer given by the other party to defend themselves.
A person appointed to collect evidence outside the court or tribunal.

99.watch: People often think files can be thrown away after a case ends, but they must be kept as permanent records.

100.summary: This rule tells you what items must be kept in a process file. A process file is a collection of official documents for a case. It helps keep all paperwork organized in one place.
points: It must contain an index.
It must include any power of attorney or vakalatnama.
It must have summons, related affidavits, and witness applications.
It must also hold letters for calling records and other papers like postal acknowledgements.
100.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited is fighting a legal case at the tribunal. Their lawyer prepares the official folder for the court. To follow the rules, the lawyer makes sure the folder contains an index page at the front, the signed vakalatnama showing the lawyer can act for the company, the official summons papers, and the postal receipts showing letters were delivered. Everything is neatly organized inside this single process file.

terms.meaning: An official folder or file that holds all the documents related to a legal case.
A written document that gives a lawyer the authority to represent a client.
A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence.

100.watch: Do not confuse this file with the main company registry records, as this is only for case-related papers.

101.summary: This rule tells us what papers must be kept inside the execution file. The file is a collection of records about carrying out a tribunal order. Everything from the index to the final result must be included.
points: The file must have an index.
It must contain the order sheet and the execution application.
It must include all processes and related papers.
It must record any transmission of the order to a civil court and the final result.
101.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited wanted to carry out an official order through the tribunal. The clerk started the official execution file for the case. First, the clerk placed the index at the very front. Next, they added the order sheet, the formal execution application, and all connected papers. When the tribunal sent the order to a civil court, a record of that transmission went into the file. Finally, once the process ended, the result of the execution was added to complete the record.

terms.meaning: a folder or collection of documents that tracks how a tribunal order is carried out
a chronological record of all orders passed in a case

102.summary: This rule explains how to arrange documents for various extra applications in a legal filing. All these miscellaneous applications must go into a single file with a specific order of papers. This keeps the paperwork organized.
points: Put all miscellaneous applications into only one file.
Place a title page right at the front of the file.
Arrange the diary, applications, supporting affidavit, order sheet, and other documents immediately after the title page.
102.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited needs to submit several extra requests to the tribunal. Instead of creating separate folders for each request, the company gathers all the paperwork into one single file. Following the rules, they place a clear title page at the very beginning. Right behind this title page, they neatly stack the diary, the miscellaneous applications, the supporting affidavit, the order sheet, and all the remaining documents in the exact order required.

terms.meaning: Various extra requests or motions filed during a legal proceeding.
A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence.
A chronological record of the court's or tribunal's orders and proceedings.

102.watch: Do not create multiple separate files for different miscellaneous applications.

103.summary: This rule explains how long documents and records handled by the Tribunal must be kept. Physical records in the record room must be kept for five years after the final order. However, the general records of petitions, applications, and orders must be kept by the Registry for fifteen years.
points: Physical records in the record room must be kept for five years after the final order.
The Registry must maintain the records of petitions, applications, and orders for fifteen years after the final order.
103.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an application at the Tribunal, which finally passed its order. As required by the rules, the physical records of this case placed in the record room must be carefully preserved for a period of five years. Meanwhile, the Registry of the Tribunal will maintain the overall record of this petition, including the final directions and orders, for a total period of fifteen years following the final order.

terms.meaning: A specialized legal body set up to deal with specific types of cases and disputes.
The administrative office of the Tribunal responsible for maintaining records and handling paperwork.

103.watch: Do not confuse the five-year preservation rule for physical records in the record room with the fifteen-year maintenance rule for general records by the Registry.

104.summary: This rule explains how records are kept and destroyed in the Record Room. A designated officer must check incoming records within three days and make an index. Once the preservation period ends, the Registrar will weed out the records.
points: A designated officer is responsible for records sent to the Record Room.
The officer must check the records and make an index within three days.
The Registrar destroys records once their preservation period is over.
104.example: At Alpha Solutions Private Limited, a box of old legal files was sent to the Record Room. Mr. Rao, the designated officer, received the box and carefully checked every document. Within three days, he finished reviewing the files and prepared a complete index. Years later, when the specific time period for keeping these records under rule 103 finally expired, the Registrar properly removed and destroyed the old files.

terms.meaning: an organized list or guide used to find records easily
to remove and destroy unwanted or old records

104.watch: People often confuse who checks the records initially with who finally destroys them.

105.summary: When the Tribunal issues a notice for a case, copies of the main filing, supporting affidavit, and any ordered documents must be sent to the other side. These copies must include specific filing details, contact information of the legal representative, and any interim orders. The Tribunal may also permit the party to deliver the notice directly by hand.
points: Copies of the appeal, petition, supporting affidavit, and other ordered documents must be served with the notice.
The served copies must show the presentation date, authorized representative's details, and any interim orders.
The Tribunal can allow a party to deliver the notice directly by hand, known as Dasti service.
The party must file proof of delivery and the acknowledgement with the Registry before the given date.
105.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal issued a notice and permitted Meera Textiles to deliver the notice directly by hand to the other party, a process known as Dasti service. Meera Textiles prepared the copies containing the presentation date and their representative's address, along with the supporting affidavit. After handing these over to the other side, Meera Textiles properly filed the proof of service and acknowledgement with the Registry before the scheduled hearing date, following all the required rules.

terms.meaning: A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation for use as evidence in court.
An application made to a court or tribunal during the course of a legal action.
Hand delivery of a court notice or summons directly by the party concerned.

105.watch: Do not forget to file the proof of service with the Registry before the date fixed for the return of notice.

106.summary: This rule explains what you must do when the Tribunal tells you to serve a notice or summons yourself using private service. You need to send copies of your documents by registered post or courier to the other side unless they already received them. Finally, you must file an affidavit of service with proof before the hearing date.
points: Send a copy of your appeals, petitions, or applications by registered post or courier if ordered by private service.
Skip this sending step only if the other side was already served in advance.
File an affidavit of service with proof of acknowledgement before the date fixed for hearing.
106.example: Aarav filed a petition at the tribunal against Apex Builders Private Limited. The tribunal ordered private service for the notice. Aarav had not given the papers to Apex Builders in advance. Therefore, Aarav sent a copy of the petition through a courier service. Before the hearing date arrived, Aarav filed an affidavit of service along with the proof of acknowledgement to show that the delivery was duly arranged.

terms.meaning: An official order or notice telling someone to appear or respond in a legal proceeding.
A written statement confirming that documents were properly delivered to the other party.

106.watch: People often forget to file the proof of acknowledgement before the hearing date.

107.summary: This rule explains what happens if a legal notice cannot be delivered. When a notice is returned unserved, the Registry must post this information and the reason on its notice board. The person who filed the case or their representative must then take steps to send a fresh notice within seven days.
points: If a notice comes back unserved, the Registry puts a note on its notice board with the reason.
The applicant, petitioner, or their representative must act.
Fresh steps to serve the notice must be taken within seven days of the notification.
107.example: Aarav filed a petition at the tribunal involving Zenith Enterprises Private Limited. The tribunal sent a notice to Zenith, but it was returned unserved because the company had moved. The Registry immediately posted this unserved notice and the reason on its notice board. Within seven days of that notification appearing on the board, Aarav and his authorized representative took steps to send the notice afresh to Zenith's correct address.

terms.meaning: The office or administrative department of the tribunal that handles official papers and filings.
When an official notice or document fails to reach or be delivered to the intended person.
The person who officially asks the tribunal for something by filing a case.

107.watch: Remember that the seven-day deadline starts from the date the notification is put on the notice board, not from the date the notice was first returned.

108.summary: This rule explains what happens if a notice cannot be delivered to the other side and you miss the deadline to fix it. The official called the Registrar will send your case to the Tribunal panel. The panel will then decide whether to give more instructions or dismiss your case.
points: A notice is sent to the other side but returns unserved.
The applicant fails to take necessary steps within the time ordered by the Tribunal.
The Registrar posts the case before the Bench for further directions or dismissal.
108.example: Meera Textiles Private Limited filed a case at the Tribunal against an opposing party. The Tribunal sent a notice, but it came back unserved. The Tribunal ordered Meera Textiles Private Limited to take new steps by a specific date. However, Meera Textiles Private Limited missed this deadline. Because of this failure, the Registrar sent the file to the Bench. The Bench will now decide whether to give new instructions or dismiss the case entirely.

terms.meaning: A special official body that settles company law disputes.
An official who manages the administrative work and records of the Tribunal.

108.watch: Do not assume a specific time period for taking steps, as the rule only refers to the period ordered by the Tribunal.

109.summary: This rule tells the judicial branch of the Registry how to keep track of legal notices sent to respondents. They must write specific details in a special section of the order sheet called 'Notes of the Registry'. This helps everyone know when notices were sent, served, returned, or if new steps are needed.
points: The judicial branch of the Registry must record notice details in the order sheet.
